raw_observations: Goroutines are lightweight (small growable initial stack), scheduled M:N onto OS threads by the runtime, enabling hundreds of thousands of concurrent goroutines cheaply.
Channels are a built-in typed primitive with direct syntax (chan, <-, select), implementing CSP-style message passing as a core language construct rather than a library addition.
select gives native multi-way non-blocking channel coordination; the standard-library context package provides pervasive cancellation/timeout propagation conventions.
Data-race detection is built into the toolchain (go run/test -race) via a first-party dynamic detector, giving strong diagnosability though it is dynamic rather than a static guarantee.

Go's type system does not statically prevent data races or enforce cross-goroutine ownership; shared mutable state via pointers/maps/slices can race without a compile error, unlike Rust's Send/Sync static concurrency safety.
sync package (Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, atomic) supplements channels, giving a layered set of primitives (message passing + shared-memory sync) rather than forcing a single paradigm.

Adversarial corpus includes deep-recursion/large-file cases (e.g. ADV-21 variants at depth 1000/10000 and 200KB source) exercising goroutine stack growth and scheduler robustness under adversarial nesting.
No async/await function-coloring problem: goroutines make concurrent and sequential code look identical.
Scheduler is cooperative-preemptive since Go 1.14 (signal-based async preemption), closing an earlier gap where tight non-yielding loops could starve the scheduler.
metric.concurrency.scoring_rationale: Normalized 0-100, 100=best. Go's concurrency model (goroutines + channels + select integrated into language syntax, plus first-party race detector and mature preemptive scheduler) is one of the strongest intrinsic concurrency designs among mainstream languages: low ceremony, uniform sync/async code shape. Deduction from a perfect score reflects the lack of compile-time data-race prevention (no ownership/borrow model), meaning shared-memory correctness still depends on discipline and runtime tooling rather than the type system, unlike languages with static Send/Sync-style guarantees.

raw_observations: Go's primary FFI mechanism is cgo, allowing calling C functions via `import "C"` pseudo-package with inline C in comments.

cgo introduces significant per-call overhead (goroutine-to-OS-thread transition, stack switching), roughly tens of ns and up, making tight-loop FFI expensive compared to zero-cost C interop in Rust, Zig, C/C++.
cgo breaks normal Go tooling: cross-compilation needs a C cross-compiler and CGO_ENABLED=1, static analysis coverage is incomplete for embedded C snippets.
No first-party lightweight non-cgo mechanism exists for calling arbitrary shared libraries; third-party pure-Go workarounds exist but signal an underlying language-level gap.

Passing Go pointers to C requires care due to the moving/relocating GC; cgo enforces pointer-passing rules at runtime, adding correctness burden absent in languages with non-relocating GC or manual memory management.
Struct/type marshaling between Go and C is manual (C.struct_X, C.CString/C.GoString, explicit frees) with no automatic ownership/lifetime tracking.
Go supports exporting Go functions to C via //export and building c-shared/c-archive artifacts, giving two-way interoperability -- a genuine positive.
No direct C++ ABI interop; C++ libraries require an extern C shim layer, an added indirection not required in Rust (bindgen), Zig, or C++ itself.

Reviewed programs/go/adversarial and programs/go/micro corpora: no dedicated cgo/FFI stress case present in this snapshot; assessment based on documented language-level cgo design properties, consistent with the methodology split of FFI DESIGN quality (Language Quality) from breadth of working external integrations (Ecosystem).
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.scoring_rationale: Normalized 0-100, 100=best. Go provides a working bidirectional C FFI (cgo) with runtime pointer-safety guardrails and two-way export capability, meriting above-median credit. However it is markedly costlier per call, weakens pure-Go toolchain/cross-compilation guarantees, requires manual marshaling/lifetime management, and lacks native C++ interop -- intrinsic language/toolchain design costs. Score reflects a workable but second-tier FFI design relative to languages with zero-cost/native C ABI interop (Rust, Zig, C/C++).
